nodes.description: Standard multidrug antituberculous therapy, as for pulmonary tuberculosis. In the reported child, rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide for two months followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for four months produced lesion healing.

evidence.reference_title: Cutaneous tuberculosis chancre: case description in a child.
evidence.snippet: After a trial treatment for tuberculosis (Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide for two months; Rifampicin and Isoniazid for four months) was initiated, the patient showed significant lesion improvement, with local healing

evidence.reference_title: Cutaneous tuberculosis chancre: case description in a child.
evidence.snippet: Treatment is similar to that of pulmonary forms of the disease.

nodes.description: As delayed-type hypersensitivity develops, the Th1 response drives macrophage differentiation into epithelioid and multinucleated (Langhans-type) giant cells that organize into granulomas with central caseous necrosis - the histopathologic hallmark that confirms the diagnosis. This is the disorder-specific instance of the conserved granuloma_formation central effector, with M. tuberculosis as the persistent stimulus.

evidence.reference_title: Cutaneous tuberculosis chancre: case description in a child.
evidence.snippet: A wedge biopsy of the larger lesion was performed, which showed a granulomatous inflammatory process with areas of caseous necrosis, lymphohistiocytic inflammatory infiltrate, and Langerhans-type giant cells, favoring the diagnosis of tuberculosis.

evidence.reference_title: Cutaneous tuberculosis: epidemiologic, etiopathogenic and clinical aspects - part I.
evidence.snippet: The chronic presence of these interleukins stimulating macrophages will ultimately cause their differentiation into epithelioid and giant cells that will organized themselves, to greater or lesser extent, into granulomas according to individual host factors.

nodes.description: Central caseous necrosis within the granulomatous lesion breaks down the overlying epidermis to produce a friable, painless ulcer. Over three to twelve months the lesion tends to heal with atrophic scarring; untreated, it can occasionally progress to lupus vulgaris, scrofuloderma, or miliary dissemination.

evidence.reference_title: Cutaneous tuberculosis: epidemiologic, etiopathogenic and clinical aspects - part I.
evidence.snippet: healing may occur between three and 12 months, leaving atrophic scarring and calcification in regional lymph nodes.

evidence.snippet: if anti-tuberculous medications are not implemented, there is potential risk of developing complications such as lupus vulgaris, scrofuloderma or dissemination (acute miliary TB).

nodes.description: Within weeks of the chancre, bacilli drain through the lymphatics to the regional lymph nodes, producing regional lymphadenopathy. The chancre plus the enlarged draining nodes constitute the cutaneous primary complex, the skin equivalent of the Ghon complex of primary pulmonary tuberculosis.

evidence.snippet: After 3 to 8 weeks from the onset of TB chancre, there is often bacilli dissemination through the lymph and lymph nodes, analogous to what happens in the lungs with Gohn's complex.

evidence.reference_title: Cutaneous tuberculosis chancre: case description in a child.
evidence.snippet: Cutaneous tuberculosis chancre constitutes a rare form of CTB and is equivalent to the primary pulmonary complex.

nodes.description: The classic chancre is a firm, painless papule or nodule that breaks down into a friable ulcer with a granular base; note that an individual case may be tender.

nodes.description: Local trauma breaches the skin barrier and introduces M. tuberculosis into the dermis of a host with no prior TB sensitization. The absence of pre-existing immunity is the defining host condition of the chancre.

evidence.reference_title: Cutaneous tuberculosis: epidemiologic, etiopathogenic and clinical aspects - part I.
evidence.snippet: it develops in individuals not previously sensitized to the mycobacterium, occurring most often in children in endemic areas of low vaccination coverage.

nodes.description: With no adaptive immunity to contain them, inoculated bacilli are taken up by dermal macrophages and neutrophils and multiply locally as a multibacillary lesion (numerous acid-fast bacilli on early histology), producing a firm, painless papule or nodule about two to four weeks after inoculation.
